content: H2N2 is a subtype of the Influenza A virus, which is sometimes referred to as the bird flu virus. This virus has undergone mutations, resulting in various strains, including the Asian Flu strain (now extinct in the wild), H3N2, and other strains found in avian species. It is also suspected to have caused a human pandemic in 1889. The Asian Flu was a Category 2 influenza pandemic caused by an avian influenza virus. It originated in China in early 1956 and persisted until 1958. This virus emerged from a genetic mutation in wild ducks, which combined with a pre-existing human influenza strain. The virus was first identified in Guizhou, China. It subsequently spread to Singapore in February 1957, reached Hong Kong by April, and arrived in the United States by June of the same year. The death toll in the United States was approximately 69,800. Global infection estimates vary widely, ranging from 1 million to 4 million cases. The Asian Flu was caused by the H2N2 strain of Influenza A, a designation that refers to the specific configuration of the hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) proteins on the virus's surface. A vaccine was developed in 1957 to mitigate the outbreak. Over time, the H2N2 strain evolved through antigenic shift into the H3N2 strain, which caused a milder pandemic from 1968 to 1969. Both the H2N2 and H3N2 pandemic strains contained RNA segments derived from avian influenza viruses. While the 1957 (H2N2) and 1968 (H3N2) pandemic influenza viruses clearly arose through genetic reassortment between human and avian influenza viruses, the virus responsible for the 1918 Spanish Flu pandemic appears to have been entirely derived from an avian source, as noted by Belshé in 2005. Between October 2004 and February 2005, approximately 3,700 test kits containing the 1957 H2N2 virus were inadvertently distributed worldwide by the College of American Pathologists (CAP). The decision to include the 1957 H2N2 strain, rather than a less virulent avian influenza subtype, was made by the company Meridian, which believed the virus to be safe. At the time, the virus was classified as a Biosafety Level 2 (BSL-2) agent, meaning it could legally be used in such test kits. However, before the issue came to light, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) had already recommended reclassifying the H2N2 virus as a BSL-3 agent, which would require stricter handling protocols to prevent airborne contamination and respiratory exposure. CDC Director Dr. Julie Gerberding promised to expedite the reclassification process. The CDC determines biosafety classifications in collaboration with the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Following the discovery of the distribution error, the U.S. government ordered the destruction of all vials containing the H2N2 strain. By April 21, 2005, CDC officials reported that 99% of the samples had been destroyed. On April 25, news reports confirmed that the last remaining samples outside the United States had been destroyed at the American University of Beirut in Lebanon, after being located at the Beirut airport. Earlier reports indicated that H2N2 samples had been sent to 3,747 laboratories under CAP's oversight and to approximately 2,700 additional labs certified by other organizations. Of the CAP-distributed samples, all but about 75 were sent to laboratories within the United States. In the United States, there is no federal regulation specifically governing the 1957 H2N2 flu strain. Some U.S. laboratories retain this potentially deadly strain in their viral libraries.
